seo.title: Karmic tail 3 7 22 compatibility: meaning for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 3 7 22 compatibility: The Empress, The Chariot and The Fool — what the three cards say about a couple and why Justice always stands at the centre.

title: The 3-7-22 karmic tail in compatibility: a home, a road and the edge of the roof
short: For a couple with the 3-7-22 tail, the three cards make a route: The Empress is the home, The Chariot is the road, The Fool is the edge beyond which the whole world opens. The riddle is that such couples often walk the whole route and end up exactly where they started. The answer is written in the cards themselves: the main task of this union is a freedom the two choose for themselves — not an escape, and not a retreat out of fear.

sections.h2: The fairy tale in which the couple recognises itself
paragraphs: In 1845 Hans Christian Andersen published "The Shepherdess and the Chimney-Sweep" (in Danish, "Hyrdinden og Skorsteensfeieren"). On a table under the mirror stand two china figures: a shepherdess with golden shoes, a red rose and a crook, and a chimney-sweep with his ladder. Close by stands an old porcelain mandarin three times their size, who can nod his head and says he is the shepherdess's grandfather. In the middle of an old carved chest a little man is carved, with a goat's hind legs, little horns and a long beard; the children call him General-Headquarters-Hindquarters-Gives-Orders-Front-and-Rear-Sergeant-Billygoat-Legs. He asks for the shepherdess's hand, the grandfather nods, and the wedding is set for that night.

The lovers run. They climb down from the table, hide in a drawer, climb out, make their way through the stove and up the chimney, sit down on its rim — and see the starry sky and all the roofs of the town. The shepherdess weeps: "The wide world is too big." The two climb back down. The grandfather, running after them, has fallen off the table and broken into three pieces. He is glued together, a rivet is put through his neck, and he can no longer nod. Billygoat-Legs never gets his answer, and the porcelain couple stays side by side.

The three scenes of the tale are the three cards of the tail, in the same order. The table under the mirror is The Empress. The way through the stove and the chimney is The Chariot. The rim of the chimney above the wide world is The Fool. The nodding grandfather, on whom the decision depends, is Justice at the centre of the couple. And Billygoat-Legs' proposal against the two's own choice is the fork in the values: The Devil or The Lovers.

The tale also has a mirror scene. The runaways hide in a drawer of the window-seat. Inside lie three or four decks of cards, not quite complete, and a little puppet theatre where a play is on. The queens of every suit sit in the front row fanning themselves with tulips, and behind them the knaves line up, "showing that they had heads both at the top and at the bottom, as face cards do have" (here and below the tale is quoted in Jean Hersholt's translation). The play is about two people who are not allowed to marry, and it makes the shepherdess cry "because it was so like her own story". A person who has calculated compatibility and is looking at the three cards of the tail is sitting in the same drawer. And every card, like a knave, has two heads: what holds the couple together in the plus stops it in the minus.

One caveat. In the tale the cards are handed out to the characters like parts in a puppet show: the shepherdess wants to go home, the sweep knows the way. In a living couple all three cards belong to both, and gender decides nothing here. Today one pulls towards the roof and the other asks to go back to the shelf; a year later it is the other way round.

sections.h2: The Empress at the entry: "having been placed there, they had become engaged"
paragraphs: Andersen explains how this union begins in a single sentence: "They had both been put on the table where they stood and, having been placed there, they had become engaged because they suited each other exactly. Both were young, both were made of the same porcelain, and neither could stand a shock." Not a meeting and not a choice, but a place. They were put on the same table, and that was enough.

The Empress at the entry to the task is the wish with which the couple enters a shared life. For Lisovskaya, the key to the Three in a couple is fertility, abundance and growth: such two meet in order to grow something together, and sometimes in order to thaw after earlier relationships that went wrong. In life it looks very simple. Within a month a rented flat turns into a home: plants on the windowsill, a shared blanket, a Sunday pie, talk about where the nursery or the business will go. The two find a common language fastest when they talk about the nest. The happiest arguments of the first years are about curtains.

Waite calls The Empress the Earthly Paradise and a refuge: "She is not Regina coeli, but she is still refugium peccatorum", the refuge of sinners. The table under the mirror is such a refuge: it is warm there, with golden shoes and a rose. In Waite's divinatory list this card has "fruitfulness, action, initiative" side by side with "difficulty, doubt", and reversed there is one more word — "vacillation". That is the shepherdess's whole line. The initiative is hers: "Please let's run away into the big, wide world." So is the doubt: "It looks very black in there." And the vacillation will come on the rim of the chimney.

The most exact clue is one sentence that the shepherdess says twice. On the table: "I'll never be happy until we are out in the big, wide world." On the roof: "I'll never be happy until I stand there again, just as before." The same words, the opposite direction. This is how the entry point of a couple's tail works. It stands on the line of tasks, so a shared wish can turn into resistance. The dream of a nest of their own first pushes the couple onto the road: away from other people's rules, to build something of their own. Then the same dream pulls them back: "we're fine where we are".

The Empress has her own scenes in the minus. Comfort one is afraid to lose, so that any suggestion of change sounds like a threat. Prosperity measured by who has brought more into the home. Relatives who feel entitled to decide because they once helped. Among the tasks of the Three, Lisovskaya names getting out from under the influence of relatives and leaving childishness behind. In the tale the grandfather "claimed that this gave him authority over her", although "he couldn't prove it".

sections.h2: The Chariot in the middle: "I'll do just what you want me to"
paragraphs: The middle of the tail shows how the couple travels from the wish to the task. The 3-7-22 couple travels by chariot: in motion, in a rush, with a clear direction and with someone holding the reins.

In the tale the reins belong to the sweep. "My way lies up through the chimney," he says. "Once we get there, I'll know what to do." Then comes a road that Waite would call a trial: his charioteer is conquest "in certain trials of initiation" too. Through the stove, through the stovepipe "where it was pitch-black night", up a terribly steep way. The sweep "lifted her up, held her safe, and found the best places for her little porcelain feet". Above them a star shines down "as if it wished to show them the way". The first two words in Waite's divinatory list for The Chariot are "succour, providence". The tale has both: the hand that lifts and the star that guides.

Lisovskaya writes about the Seven in a couple almost literally about these two: such couples often move house in search of "a home of their own", and among their tasks is deciding on a move together. Andersen's tale is the story of a move that never happened. In the middle of this tail a couple often lives like a crew: a mortgage and a renovation, a move to another city, two jobs, a business of their own, a marathon towards the first big income. The Chariot is good at one thing — taking an obstacle. The two did get through the chimney.

This card has a dark side too, and the tale shows it. The sweep says "yes" twice. The first time at the start: "I'll do just what you want me to," he tells her. "Let's run away right now." The second time on the roof, when the shepherdess begs to go home: "he had to do as she said, though he thought it was the wrong thing to do." The one who has a way of his own hands over the reins twice. Lisovskaya names this among the minuses and tasks of the Seven: one partner adjusts to the other, a partner is expected to give up their own goals for someone else's. The chariot is driven by the one who knows the chimney, and the direction is set by the one who cries. Who really decides in this couple, nobody knows — the two least of all.

The second dark side is running instead of talking. In the whole tale nobody ever speaks to the grandfather. The two hide in a drawer, think of climbing into the pot-pourri vase of rose petals and lavender to "throw salt in his eyes", climb the chimney — but never walk up to the table to say "no". Wen notes that the Chariot person "likes to appear in control, but has a tendency to run from his or her problems". Couples with the 3-7-22 tail know this: it is easier to start a renovation, change city or job, than to say out loud, just once, what does not suit them.

sections.h2: The Fool, the main task: the rim of the chimney and a world too big
paragraphs: The couple's main task is The Fool. This point is read mostly through the minus: what does not work for the couple and what it has to learn.

The tale brings its heroes exactly to this card. "Overhead was the starry sky, and spread before them were all the housetops in the town." Waite describes The Fool at the same point: a young man "pauses at the brink of a precipice among the great heights of the world; he surveys the blue distance before him—its expanse of sky rather than the prospect below." And: "The edge which opens on the depth has no terror." In Andersen two sit on the same edge, but they look in different ways. The sweep is at home on the roof: this is his way. The shepherdess sees all the roofs of the town spread before her, and she is frightened: "The poor shepherdess had never thought it would be like that."

One more clue. Waite writes that The Fool is "a prince of the other world on his travels through this one". Andersen writes of the sweep at the very start that "he was only an ornamental chimney-sweep. If the china-makers had wanted to, they could just as easily have turned him out as a prince". A prince of roofs and chimneys, dressed up in soot, is this couple's Fool — the part of it that feels cramped at home.

The tale shows the price of freedom in one detail: the shepherdess "sobbed so many tears that the gilt washed off her sash". The Empress's gold does not stay on up on the roof. Then comes the sentence where all the cards of the tail meet: "I followed you faithfully out into the world, and if you love me the least bit you'll take me right home." In it are the home, the road, the tally of concessions and the love used to pay for the way back.

The Fool in the minus, for Lisovskaya, is an easy start and trouble as soon as serious steps come up. Down below, the sweep asks the shepherdess whether she has thought "about how big it is, and that we can never come back here". "I have," she says. On the rim of the chimney it turns out she had not. A modern couple has its own chimney rim: signing for a flat, getting married, deciding to have a child, leaving on a contract abroad, quitting a job for a business of their own. They reached the edge easily, and at the edge one of them says the world is too big.

The Fool's minus has other faces too. A relationship with no defined status: "we live together, we'll see". Two people under one roof, each on their own, like neighbours. Running from difficulty with reproaches to the partner: "I climbed into that chimney for you." A freedom with no room for commitments — or strict rules for the other while one's own are not kept.

It matters that the tale does not make the return itself the mistake. Wen describes The Fool as a fork in the path: "One fork will lead to attainment (flying, transcending the cliff) and the other will lead to likely demise (falling off the cliff)." For the reversed card she even says that "it would behoove the Seeker to turn back and take the other fork". The mistake of the shepherdess and the sweep is not that they came back but how. She came back out of fear and on the condition "if you love me"; he, "though he thought it was the wrong thing to do". Neither of them chose the return. Waite's Fool will come back too, but "by another path after many days". The porcelain couple came back by the same path, the same night.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: scales that bring everything back to zero
paragraphs: The centre of the couple's matrix is the atmosphere inside the union, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. For couples with the 3-7-22 tail it holds 8, Justice. Not for most of them — for all.

In the plus this is a good atmosphere: honesty, a clear agreement, duties shared equally, "a cool head and a warm heart", as Lisovskaya writes of the Eight in a couple. Such couples take a long time to look each other over and a long time to settle in, but afterwards they can be relied on.

The tale shows how these scales work inside the tail. The shepherdess's sentence on the roof is built like a calculation, and in Andersen's Danish it is even more symmetrical: "now I have followed you out into the wide world, now you may follow me home again, if you care for me at all" (my translation). A concession for a concession, a step for a step. The scales balance exactly, and the couple ends up at zero. Back on the table, the sweep sums up: "Back where we started from. We could have saved ourselves a lot of trouble." The Danish is sharper still: "See how far we got!" An honest exchange of concessions does not move this union a single step. It returns it to where it was.

Then comes guilt. Seeing the grandfather on the floor, the shepherdess wrings her hands: "poor old grandfather is all broken up, and it's entirely our fault." Among the tasks of Justice in a couple, Lisovskaya names admitting one's own fault instead of blaming everyone, and learning to forgive. This task has a reverse side: guilt holds people in place as well as glue does.

And finally the grandfather himself, whose nod decides the couple's fate. In English such a figure is a nodding mandarin; Russian calls it kitaisky bolvanchik, the "little Chinese dummy", and uses the name for anyone who nods along: the porcelain head rocks and agrees with whatever is said. He "couldn't prove" he was her grandfather, yet he nodded to Billygoat-Legs, and that was enough. Waite's reversed Justice includes the words "bias, excessive severity". In a 3-7-22 couple anything can stand in the grandfather's place: relatives, "the way things are done", a shared ledger kept in the head, one's own inner judge. Justice at the centre easily turns into a nodding mandarin that nods on behalf of both.

This centre also has its own story in numbers. In 98% of such couples the partners' personal centres are 3 and 5: one has The Empress at the centre of their personal chart, the other The Hierophant, keeper of rules and of blessing. In the remaining 2% they are 8 and 18. One partner's comfort and the other's sense of rules together give the couple an atmosphere of scales.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Lovers or Billygoat-Legs
paragraphs: The couple's values (the spiritual purpose) are what the union exists for. For the 3-7-22 tail there are only two options here: The Lovers for 65.2% of couples and The Devil for 34.8%. The tale gives both of them a face.

The Lovers is the card of choice. In the story of the shepherdess and the sweep it is the main question nobody asks: are they together because they chose each other, or because, "having been placed there", they simply got engaged? Waite writes that the old Lovers card "is said to have been entitled Simulacrum fidei, the symbol of conjugal faith". The china figures on the table are exactly such a symbol, literally. Among Waite's reversed meanings is "marriage frustrated" — the play in the drawer, where two lovers are not allowed to marry. For a couple with The Lovers in its values, the path is to turn the image into a choice: not just to stand side by side, but one day to tell each other that they stand here because they want to.

The Devil in the values is the theme of who belongs to whom. Billygoat-Legs, with his little horns and goat's legs, wears the usual face of the devil in European fairy tales. He is rich: "He has the whole chest full of silver, and who knows what else he's got hidden away in his secret drawers?" — and in there he already has "eleven china wives". His last question is an owner's question: "Am I to have her, or am I not?" But Waite has a phrase that explains Billygoat-Legs too: he who is exalted above the chained figures "is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman". Billygoat-Legs is carved into the chest. In the whole tale he only jumps and shouts "They're running away! They're running away!", but he never leaves his place: at the end he "was standing where he always stood, looking thoughtful". The threat the two fled through the chimney could never have caught them. Only the nodding mandarin gave chase — and broke.

Lisovskaya's final thought on the fifteenth energy in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. For a couple with The Devil in its values the lesson lies here: the dark chest full of silver — comfort, money, the fear of loss — frightens more than it can hold. And it holds only those who believe in it themselves.

sections.h2: How the 3-7-22 tail is calculated for a couple: an example and the clues in the numbers
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. An example: the partners were born on 05.05.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first has the personal karmic tail 18-6-15, the second 12-19-7. Add them point by point:

The couple's middle is not derived from the two outer numbers: it is the sum of the two personal middles. The 3-7-22 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 292 (0.342%) and ranks 67th of the 97 couple tails. No couple tail is made of the same three numbers in another order.
Going through all dates since 1900 shows that this tail is assembled from only three combinations of the partners' personal tails:

Share of such couples
What The Fool is made of

paragraphs: This table holds three clues. First: in such couples the entry is always exactly 30, the middle exactly 25 and the main task exactly 22, with no reduction — a couple's Fool comes only from an exact sum. Second: neither partner has The Fool in their personal tail, and in 38% of such couples it is absent from every main point of both personal charts. The freedom the couple is learning does not come from either of the two: it is born only between them. Third, a coincidence that is hard to pass by. In 69% of couples The Fool is made of one partner's Chariot and the other's Devil, 7 + 15. That is exactly the tale: flight (The Chariot) from Billygoat-Legs (The Devil) brings the two to the edge of the wide world. It is a coincidence of numbers, not a law, but the picture is exact.

The example couple has two more marks. The Fool stands not only in its main task but also at the point "What fills" — this happens in 5.4% of couples with this tail. And at the point "Where it sparks", which shows what causes serious quarrels, stands 21, The World — as in 4% of such couples. So freedom both gives this couple strength and is exactly where it may spark: around the big world — plans, moves, going out into it.

A personal 3-7-22 tail exists too: 1,353 dates since 1900 have it. But that is a different calculation, with different roles for the points. If 3-7-22 appears in compatibility, it has to be read by the couple's roles.
Put the cards of the tail together with the centre and the values, and Andersen's tale becomes a circle that a 3-7-22 couple can go round more than once.

ol: **The nest.** The couple is joined by the wish for something of their own: a home, plenty, a shared business. The two stand side by side because that is how things turned out, and they are happy.
**Someone else's decision.** A nod hangs over the nest: relatives, circumstances, "the way things are done". Nobody dares to name it aloud.

**The dash.** The couple throws itself into motion: a move, a renovation, a new project. One knows the way and leads, the other holds on. The one who leads puts their own goals aside: "I'll do just what you want me to."
**The edge.** The couple reaches the freedom it set out for — and one of them is frightened: "the wide world is too big".
**The tally.** The way back is paid for with a concession and with love: I followed you, now you take me home, if you love me.
**Zero.** The couple returns by the same path to the same place, with guilt on top. "Back where we started from."

**The rivet.** The question of the couple's status is closed not by the couple but by a circumstance: money, a contract, someone's silence. The couple thanks the rivet, and everything stays as it was.

paragraphs: The last step looks like a happy ending, and in the tale it is one: the two keep on loving each other "until the day they broke". Only their freedom came not from their will but from grandfather's rivet. The tale begins with the two being placed side by side and ends with them staying side by side. In the whole story the two themselves decided nothing.

sections.h2: How to break the circle: freedom with a way back
paragraphs: For this couple The Fool does not demand leaving home at all costs, nor staying at all costs. Its task is for the two to decide it themselves — on the rim of the chimney, aloud and together.

ul: **Talk to "the grandfather" before running.** Name who or what nods on the couple's behalf: relatives, money, habit, an inner judge. Saying "no" at the table is easier than climbing the chimney later.

**Do not demand the whole world at once.** The sweep's question about "how big it is, and that we can never come back here" puts the couple before the whole world in one go. The world really is too big to enter in one night. One can go out to the edge more often and for short spells: a trip, a trial month, a small shared risk. That is how a big step is prepared rather than put off.
**Do not pay with love.** "If you love me" is a poor currency for decisions. A concession for which a return concession is later demanded is no longer care but a debt book.

**Each has a way of their own.** The sweep knows the chimney, the shepherdess her table. Lisovskaya advises a couple with The Chariot to walk side by side but each on their own path, and a couple with The Fool to give the partner freedom without checks and to take temporary separations calmly. One can go off to their own roofs and come back; the other can keep the home.
**Settle the status before the rivet does.** Who we are to each other and where we are going — let the couple answer that, not a circumstance that one day will stop nodding.
**Notice "I'll do just what you want me to".** When one partner agrees to everything for a long time, the bill will be presented sooner or later.

paragraphs: The strong version of 3-7-22 looks like this. The couple has a home, but it is a base, not a shelf: they leave it and come back to it. The couple starts from zero easily and finds a way out where others see a cliff — this is how Lisovskaya describes The Fool in the plus. The two are like best friends: each is self-sufficient and stays in the union by their own choice. The Empress gives them what they met for — growth and abundance. The Chariot gives them the knack of taking obstacles together. And The Fool gives them the freedom to come home by another path, no longer the people who left.

ul: **Entry to the task — 3, The Empress.** The couple is joined by the wish for a home of their own, for plenty, for something grown together. Later the same wish holds them in place.
**Middle of the task — 7, The Chariot.** The couple travels its path in motion: moves, dashes, projects, where one leads and the other holds on.
**Main task — 22, The Fool.** Learning freedom as two: taking serious steps into the unknown and not running from them, forwards or backwards.

intro: At the centre of the matrix every such couple has Justice; in the values, The Lovers or The Devil. All these cards are already laid out in one fairy tale by Andersen, from the little table under the mirror to the rim of a chimney.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 3 7 22 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the couple's task, written in three cards: The Empress at the entry (a shared wish for home and plenty), The Chariot in the middle (a path in motion, where one leads), The Fool in the main task (freedom as two). Most often this is a couple that builds a nest, moves a lot and learns to take serious steps into the unknown by itself — not by someone else's decision and not out of fear.

faq.q: Is it a difficult tail for a couple?
faq.a: A couple's tail is not a verdict and not a forecast; it shows what the two have to learn together. For 3-7-22 the difficulty is that comfort and freedom pull in different directions, and decisions are made through an exchange of concessions. The strength is the ability to start from zero, to move together and to trust each other.

faq.q: How is the couple's 3-7-22 tail different from the personal 3-7-22 tail?
faq.a: A personal 3-7-22 tail belongs to 1,353 dates since 1900 and is calculated from a single date of birth. A couple's tail is the sum of the same points of two personal matrices, and its points mean something else: the entry to the task, the middle of the task and the couple's main task. Personal readings do not carry over to the couple.

faq.q: Why do all couples with this tail have Justice at the centre?
faq.a: That is how the numbers add up. The tail is assembled from only three combinations of personal tails, and in each of them the partners' personal centres add up to 8: in 98% of couples these are 3 and 5, in 2% they are 8 and 18. So the atmosphere of such couples is a pair of scales: an honest agreement, duties shared equally and the habit of counting who gave way to whom.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether it has the 3-7-22 tail?
faq.a: Calculate the compatibility matrix from the two dates of birth and look at the couple's karmic tail. For example, partners born on 05.05.1976 and 05.07.1975 have the personal tails 18-6-15 and 12-19-7, and their point-by-point sum gives 3-7-22.

report: "Here we are," says the chimney-sweep in Andersen's tale. "Back where we started from. We could have saved ourselves a lot of trouble." He is back with his bride on the very table under the mirror they had run away from. "The Shepherdess and the Chimney-Sweep" is laid out exactly along the cards of the 3-7-22 tail: the table is The Empress, the way through the stove and up the chimney is The Chariot, the rim of the chimney above the wide world is The Fool. Justice, which stands at the centre of every such couple, is there too: the old porcelain mandarin who says he is the shepherdess's grandfather and with a nod gives her to Billygoat-Legs, the little man carved into the chest. In the tale the parts are handed out to the characters; in a living couple they are not fixed, and the pull towards the roof comes now from one, now from the other.

report.h3: Placed side by side, and so engaged

report: Andersen explains the engagement in one sentence: "having been placed there, they had become engaged because they suited each other exactly". Not a meeting and not a choice, but a place. The Empress at the entry is the shared wish: a home of their own, plenty, something grown together. The two find a common language fastest when they talk about the nest.

But this point stands on the line of tasks, and here a wish easily turns into resistance. The shepherdess says the same sentence twice. On the table: "I'll never be happy until we are out in the big, wide world." On the roof: "I'll never be happy until I stand there again, just as before." **The dream of a nest of their own first pushes the couple onto the road, then pulls it back.**

report.h3: The one who knows the way hands over the reins twice

report: The middle of the tail is The Chariot: the couple moves towards its task in motion, in a rush, and someone holds the reins. "My way lies up through the chimney… Once we get there, I'll know what to do," says the sweep, and he lifts his bride and finds the best places for her little porcelain feet. In Waite's list for The Chariot the first words are "succour, providence", and above the runaways a star really does shine down "as if it wished to show them the way". In life such a crew is easy to recognise: a mortgage and a renovation, a move to another city, two jobs, a business of their own.

Only the sweep says "yes" twice: "I'll do just what you want me to" at the start, and on the roof "he had to do as she said, though he thought it was the wrong thing to do". The chariot is driven by the one who knows the chimney, and the direction is set by the one who cries. And in the whole tale nobody ever speaks to the grandfather: climbing a chimney is easier than saying "no" at the table.

report.h3: The edge where the world is too big

report: The couple's main task is The Fool, and it is read through what does not work. "Overhead was the starry sky, and spread before them were all the housetops in the town." Waite's Fool stands at the brink of a precipice, and for him "the edge which opens on the depth has no terror". The sweep is at home on the roof: no wonder the china-makers "could just as easily have turned him out as a prince", while Waite's Fool is "a prince of the other world on his travels through this one". The shepherdess is frightened: "The wide world is too big." Her tears wash the gilt off her sash, and The Empress's gold does not stay on up on the roof.

Then comes the sentence where the whole tail meets: "I followed you faithfully out into the world, and if you love me the least bit you'll take me right home." **A concession for a concession — that is how the scales of Justice work, and they balance at zero.** The couple returns by the same path to the same place, with guilt on top: "it's entirely our fault".

A modern couple has its own chimney rim: getting married, signing for a flat, moving away, leaving a job for a business of their own. They reached the edge easily, and at the edge one of them says the world is too big. Hence a relationship with no defined status, life under one roof but apart, and reproaches like "I climbed into that chimney for you".

report.h3: A rivet instead of a decision

report: The tale ends happily. The grandfather, chasing the runaways, fell and broke; he was glued together and a rivet was put through his neck, and he was as good as new, "except that never again could he nod his head". Billygoat-Legs gets no answer, and the couple stays together. But their fate was settled not by their will but by the rivet. **The tale begins with two figures placed side by side and ends with them staying side by side.** In the whole story they themselves decided nothing.

In English such a figure is a nodding mandarin; Russian calls it kitaisky bolvanchik, the "little Chinese dummy": a head that nods to everything. In a living couple anything can stand in the grandfather's place — relatives, "the way things are done", money, one's own inner judge. Coming home is not a mistake in itself: Waite's Fool will come back too, but "by another path after many days". The porcelain couple came back by the same path, the same night, and neither of the two chose the return.

The strong version of the tail is deciding on the rim of the chimney themselves, aloud and together. Naming who nods on the couple's behalf, and saying "no" before running. Going out to the edge more often and for short spells: the world is too big to enter in one night. Not paying for decisions with the words "if you love me". Letting each other go off to their own roofs and calmly waiting for the return. Settling the status of the relationship themselves, before another rivet does it for the couple. **Then the home becomes a base rather than a shelf, and The Fool becomes the freedom to come home by another path.**

unit.title: A chimney rim above the world

captions.M: Wanting a nest of your own that later pulls you back
captions.N: Rushing ahead, handing over the reins instead of talking
captions.D: Deciding on freedom together — aloud, not out of fear

unit.meaning: Your task is to decide on freedom yourselves: not to trade concessions or wait for relatives or money to decide for you.
